Spending two days on a university campus that’s not Stanford makes me realize that society is absolutely not ready for what’s to come. Everyone’s about deer-in-the-headlights as everyone else. 

Most are still going about their old ways of doing things treating this whole “AI thing” as something that will be figured out later while also openly expressing worries about how this will have hugely disruptive impacts on society and employment over cocktails. 

How will our institutions respond to or cope with the rapid change amidst a plethora of other seismic changes like geopolitics, demographics and migration, and inflation etc etc. 

Apparently China’s economic slowdown alone has led to a sharp decrease in the enrollments of international masters students that historically help fund many of the other programs since international students pay much higher tuition than domestic esp in-state students. 

Now add on top of it the demographic aging and the disruption of AI on the value of (higher) education and institutional knowledge acquisition. 

So far this has had a counterintuitive positive impact on the top tier universities like the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, while hitting the lower tier schools much harder. We saw similar things in the commercial real estate market: new and fancy office buildings saw an increase in demand while older offices were abandoned. It remains to be seen whether this trend continues or is only a transitory substitution effect before the “income effect” takes over.

Good question! Just some informal thoughts... there's three "moats" to look at for $SIVE:

- Capacity 
- Qualifications (especially for custom DFB lasers)
- Technological

1. For capacity, they're coming online with 100M+ CW DFB lasers Q4 2027 (global supply is roughly ~608M EML/CW lasers currently per Trendforce). 

Obviously by 2027 global capacity is going to grow a lot, with $AAOI, $AVGO (3x expansion), and others coming online.  

But if you extrapolate their 2:1 statement, that implies 300m lasers/year long term coming from their own supply + external foundries. 

This is incredibly valuable during a shortage that was quoted to be 3-5 years, and $LITE stating they already have demand visibility into 2031...

And when suppliers have started to qualify many more (eg. 5-7 vendors vs. 2-3 earlier) due to bottlenecks. 

I'm sure a lot of how they achieve that staggering amount is due to their manufacturing process/yields (which is a moat). 

2. For qualifications, if you look at 70mW/100mW pluggable lines with Chinese players, I'd argue this is more generic and moreso reverting back to a capacity  argument and manufacturing process to achieve those numbers. 

Custom DFB arrays that they've been working on with Ayar (they hinted at 2-3 others back in 2023 like Celestial) take years for optical i/o related things and would be a moat if they finish quals. 

So it's not quite something you can hot swap or design out really easily for $MTSI or another company. But of course cpo scale up and such is mass volume in 2028, and we're still H2 2026. 

3. People can always compare raw specs like power output, but it's probably way way more nuanced so easier to just point toward customer statements. 

With $JBL 1.6T LRO: "I think that there's the potential for a relatively dramatic moat with our LRO part…" from Jabil's EVP, especially related to power consumption. And $SIVE is my guess sole source in this line. 

Jabil is probably the most important testament to how their lasers perform in mass production scenarios maybe around Q2 next year. 

Ayar said something similar along the lines of "we couldn't do it without Sivers" for custom implementations.

I think almost everything about my $AXTI thesis from 2025 was validated? 

From AXT's position in the InP substrate bottleneck... Being able to threaten the hyperscaler buildout (per Reuters)... 

$IQE has been flagging this as a major risk, VPEC and Taiwan epiwafer foundries have been crying over InP substrate bottlenecks. 

And there's even AXT direct confirmation of partnerships with $LITE and $COHR as the InP substrate supplier. AXT also stated $130m/quarter InP revenue capacity exiting 2027 (~$520m annualized) so that's a massive revenue inflection compared to previously. 

Now... the biggest question is: How much can AXT price hike? 

The substrates they make are just such a tiny part of the BOM... but can threaten hyperscaler buildouts with optics. 

So if they manage to price hike to $SNDK NAND degrees (which they can), then I think AXT could get re-rated a ton from here. But if they end up like Japanese ABF suppliers that are less willing to abuse their position, that's a different story.  

Will need to do more channel checks to see how that's coming along.

But at the very least, I would argue there should be some valuation baseline just due to their critical importance (eg. upstream refinery ownerships, crucible processing, etc) + existing capacity revenue without hikes. 

TLDR: 
- Bottleneck thesis was at like ~$500m MC 
- Upside now comes from price hikes due to duopoly position + ownership of upstream bottlenecks in the InP substrate manufacturing process. (which they can due to low cost of InP substrates in overall costs) 
- Uncharted territory, we'll see (also a central part of geopolitical tensions so there's always risk there).

DeFi has around $91B in TVL right now.

But how much of that money is actually protected if something goes wrong? The money set aside to cover losses is only about 0.14% of that.

We spend hours comparing vault APYs and strategies, but rarely check what happens if a protocol gets exploited. 

It’s like obsessing over a car’s horsepower and skipping the insurance.

DeFi already has protection options. The problem is that most vaults don't include them, leaving users to arrange to cover themselves.

Interestingly, @Firelightfi recently launched a different approach to this, where the vault operator sets up the cover so every depositor gets it automatically.

Here's how it works.

If a covered vault suffers an eligible exploit, five independent security firms review the incident against predefined terms. Once validated, eligible losses can be paid from the capital backing the cover, subject to coverage limits.

The money behind those payouts comes from people staking $FXRP, which is basically $XRP brought over to the Flare network. They earn rewards for taking on that risk, and there’s already 50M+ FXRP staked.

It’s live on Sentora’s USD and RWA vaults, and Veda and Upshift have plugged it in so vaults built on them can switch it on anytime.

I wouldn’t treat this as a guarantee. It only covers specific events like hacks and oracle attacks, and the terms still matter.

But having protection built into a vault, rather than making everyone arrange it separately is kinda how this should’ve worked from the start.

$1.3B in tokens unlocks in October. 

Here are the 5 I'm watching, and the 4 things that tell you whether an unlock actually dumps:

- $PUMP (Oct 11): ~$41.5M unlocking, around 1.5% of supply. Up roughly 12% over the 7 days after its previous unlock on Sep 11.

- $APT (Oct 11): ~$8.5M unlocking, around 0.6% of supply. After its previous unlock on Sep 11, APT fell roughly 7% over the next 7 days.

- $STRK (Oct 15): ~$6.2M unlocking, around 3.4% of supply. 

The ironic part? STRK gained roughly 73% in the 7 days after its Sep 14 unlock.

- $ARB (Oct 16): ~$17M unlocking, around 1.6% of supply. ARB was up roughly 69% in the week after its Sep 15 unlock.

- $ZRO (Oct 20): ~$54M unlocking, around 4% of supply. Its Sep 19 unlock was followed by roughly a 45% gain over the next 7 days.

The obvious mistake here would be looking at those September returns and assuming the same thing happens again.

A lot of that was the market. $BTC went from ~$63k in mid-August to the high $80s by Mid-September, sentiment flipped bullish, and alts caught the wave right as these unlocks were hitting.

The better question is what actually happens to the new tokens.

HYPE is the best example from this week. Its unlock looked huge on paper, but a large part of the team allocation being claimed was sold OTC to a single institutional buyer instead of immediately hitting the open market.

That’s why I’d care more about:

1. how big the unlock is vs supply
2. who receives it
3. whether those tokens move to exchanges
4. what the market is doing at the same time

For most of these, the tokens go to the team, core contributors, and strategic partners, so that part doesn't separate them much. Size does, which is why $ZRO and $STRK get most of my attention at 4% and 3.4% of supply.

Which upcoming unlock are you watching most closely?

The better question is what actually happens to the new tokens.

HYPE is the best example from this week. Its unlock looked huge on paper, but a large part of the team allocation being claimed was sold OTC to a single institutional buyer instead of immediately hitting the open market.

That’s why I’d care more about:

1. how big the unlock is vs supply
2. who receives it
3. whether those tokens move to exchanges
4. what the market is doing at the same time

For most of these, the tokens go to the team, core contributors, and strategic partners, so that part doesn't separate them much. Size does, which is why $ZRO and $STRK get most of my attention at 4% and 3.4% of supply.

Which upcoming unlock are you watching most closely?

This is everything I admired about America as a teenager growing up in France.

Michael Dell starts a company at 19 in his dorm room with $1,000, becomes a billionaire, then he and Susan commit $6.25 billion to give 25 million American children their first investment.

I remember my high school teachers blaming large corporations and their dividends. It was just accepted in the classroom: corporations were evil, dividends were evil.

And I remember thinking: wait. There’s a system where I can buy a piece of these companies, and they’ll give me money on a recurring basis?

Everyone was explaining why this was terrible, and all I could think was: I need a piece of that. If I want to escape poverty, I need to own some of these businesses.

It took me years to understand investing properly. I hope these kids get that realization much sooner.

Munger said: “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

You can explain the benefits of capitalism forever. But owning a piece of a business gives you a personal reason to understand profits, dividends, reinvestment and compounding.

Suddenly, America’s most successful companies are partly yours. Their success means something to you.

And maybe a kid who starts by asking “What do I own?” will eventually ask “What could I build?”

That’s what makes this so inspiring to me. A man who built his fortune giving millions of children a first experience of ownership, and perhaps the ambition to build something themselves.

This is the America I dreamed of.
LFG America 🇺🇸
